approach: The authors conducted a narrative review by synthesizing existing literature on CAR-T cell therapy mechanisms, gut microbiota functions, and their interactions. They analyzed data from retrospective and prospective clinical cohorts (e.g., Smith et al., Stein-Thoeringer et al.) and preclinical studies (mouse models) to identify correlations between microbial signatures and therapeutic responses/toxicities. The review categorizes findings into effects on efficacy, effects on toxicity, and potential modulation strategies (FMT, diet, metabolites).

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Synthesizes emerging evidence linking gut microbiota composition to CAR-T cell therapy outcomes (efficacy and toxicity), providing a framework for understanding microbiome-immune interactions in adoptive cell therapy.
contribution_and_limits.limits: The review is narrative and relies on heterogeneous data from different studies with varying methodologies. Many findings are based on small cohorts or animal models. Causal mechanisms are largely unproven in humans, and the review acknowledges significant inter-individual variability in microbial signatures, making generalizable biomarkers difficult to define.

key_findings.conditions: Clinical cohort of CD19 CAR-T patients; exposure to broad-spectrum antibiotics (PIM)
key_findings.finding: Antibiotic exposure prior to CAR-T therapy was associated with worse overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and increased incidence of immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) and cytokine release syndrome (CRS).

key_findings.conditions: Baseline microbiota analysis in CD19 CAR-T patients
key_findings.finding: Higher baseline microbiota diversity and enrichment of specific taxa (Ruminococcus, Faecalibacterium, Bacteroides) were positively correlated with complete response rates.

key_findings.conditions: BCMA CAR-T therapy for multiple myeloma
key_findings.finding: Differences in enrichment of Bifidobacterium, Prevotella, Sutterella, and Collinsella were observed between patients in complete remission versus partial remission.

key_findings.conditions: Vancomycin-induced dysbiosis in mouse models and human B-ALL patients
key_findings.finding: Oral vancomycin (targeting Gram-positive bacteria) led to increased CAR-T cell peak expansion and tumor response in mice, suggesting that depletion of certain Gram-positive taxa may impair antigen presentation or have complex effects distinct from broad-spectrum antibiotic impacts.
Nonoxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway was upregulated in patients with toxicities, suggesting bacterial metabolites may serve as biomarkers for side effects.

problem_or_question: To understand the role of the gut microbiota in predicting and modifying the efficacy and toxicity of CAR-T cell therapy, and to evaluate potential microbiota-based interventions to improve clinical outcomes.
research_scope: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy, gut microbiota, cancer immunotherapy efficacy and toxicity. The review covers preclinical models (mouse) and clinical cohorts (human), focusing on hematologic malignancies and solid tumors.
work_summary: This review article discusses the interplay between the gut microbiota and CAR-T cell therapy. It highlights how the gut microbiome influences both the antitumor efficacy and the adverse events (such as cytokine release syndrome [CRS] and neurotoxicity) of CAR-T treatments. The authors summarize current evidence from clinical studies and animal models, identifying specific bacterial taxa associated with treatment outcomes. Furthermore, the paper explores potential strategies to modulate the gut microbiota—such as fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), diet, prebiotics, probiotics, and metabolite supplementation—to enhance CAR-T cell efficacy and reduce toxicity, while also addressing challenges like mechanistic uncertainty and inter-individual variability.
